item.title: The Pulse: Details of incident.io’s AI spend
item.description: The resiliency startup has slashed the amount it spends on AI; down from $4,500 per dev, per month, in August, to $1,600 now.
item.dc:creator: Ivan Klaric
item.content:encoded:
Hi, this is Gergely with a bonus, free issue of the Pragmatic Engineer Newsletter. In every issue, I cover Big Tech and startups through the lens of senior engineers and engineering leaders. Today, we cover one out of five topics from the past issue of The Pulse. Full subscribers received the article below two weeks ago. If you’ve been forwarded this email, you can subscribe here.

incident.io (note: I’m an investor) is a software reliability platform founded in 2021, a year before ChatGPT, that’s obsessed with measuring everything. In that spirit, the company has shared details about AI spending, changes to PR frequency, and the ROI at the company from using AI. Thank you to Lawrence Jones and the incident.io team for sharing the data!

They have come up with the concept of the “effort point” as a way to analyse AI spend. One effort point is a medium-sized pull request written by a human or generated by an agent. The measurement is far from perfect, but it is one step more granular than looking at lines of code, and lets them compare the complexity of AI-generated PRs with those written by human devs in the past. Here’s what has changed in the last two years:

Pull request stats

At a glance:

AI agents started to generate production code in June 2025, which was around the same time as the first agent-generated got pushed at incident.io. The company has used AI-assisted IDEs since the beginning, such as GitHub Copilot and Cursor.

In June this year, a few things happened in quick succession, the incident.io team told me:

  • Claude Agents launched, making it easier to coordinate several agents running at once
  • Worktree tooling improved a lot, making it easier for agents to do parallel work on the same codebase with worktrees
  • Also around this time, more engineers realized that they should be running multiple agent sessions using different worktrees, rather than driving just one session at once.

Today, nearly 80% of PRs that ship to production include code generated by an agent:

More:

  • 2.7x headcount growth in product engineering (engineers who ship to production numbered 18 in 2024, and 50 today)
  • 3.4x PR requests shipped to production in September compared to a year ago
  • 3.6x increase in PRs with no human reviewer shipped to prod (12% to 43%)
  • 4.8x increase in the size of PRs (from 22 to 111 lines)
  • 6x “effort points” shipped to prod: “effort points” awarded by an AI model estimating the complexity of a PR, and ranking it from XS to XL.
  • 80% decrease in human comments per “effort point”
  • 60% decrease in incidents per 1,000 pull requests

Stats on release frequency:

  • 47% rise in releases/eng/day when taking headcount into account: an average of 2.8 releases/day/eng, up from 1.9 releases/day/eng in 2024
  • Oct 2026: 140 releases/day to production with 50 engineers. In Oct 2024, the figures were 35 releases/day to prod with 18 engineers

AI spend

This year, spending on AI tools is on track to be around $1.6M at the company – which is a lot! We’re talking around $2,700 per engineer each month, which puts the reliability startup among the big spenders of companies mentioned in this article. Based on that, they’ve attempted to calculate a rudimentary ROI for the spend. At present, incident.io sees AI tools as mostly positive.

AI spending peaked this summer and has been decreasing since. In July, the company spent more than $300K on AI (an annual projection of $3.6M, had it continued). Here’s the allocation:

Opus 5.5 brought a massive cost reduction. Before it, the company was spending around $4,500/engineer/month, mostly on Opus 5. But now, with the 5.5 version, the cost is down to circa $1,600. Here’s the impact of Opus 5.5 on monthly spend:

Also, the adoption of Opus 5.5 has been rapid:

Cost per “effort point” also peaked over the summer. The nice thing about the “effort point” metric is that it makes it possible to compare the cost of generating a PR to how much it cost a year ago, when the company started using AI agents. Here’s the change:

Infrastructure teams spend more tokens on the same “effort point.” A fascinating detail from incident.io comes from separating the cost of an “effort point.” The infrastructure team stands out, spending ~5x more on a medium-sized PR than almost every other team:

But why the big difference? Lawrence Jones, an engineer at incident.io, explains:

“This is a great example of why it’s hard to use a single target for cost per PR that applies universally.

Our AI team, for example, does work that can be very token-intensive such as iterating on evals. Infrastructure teams might use Claude to explore production environments or do lots of analysis or run benchmarks etc which don’t lead to PRs, so their cost per-PR looks higher.

Different types of work will simply have different cost profiles.”

Measuring ROI

Today, average spend is down at ~$1,600/engineer/month, of which around 80% is on Claude, with 20% going to Cursor. The big question: has AI made engineers more productive? Unfortunately, measuring engineering productivity in only a single dimension is fraught with hazard, but a combination of insights could give a sense of where things are headed. These are imperfect measurements with their own biases, but are still interesting.

The number of PRs shipped per engineer weekly tracks with tenure. This is a very interesting finding from incident.io. Compared to two years ago:

  • The median engineer shipped ~10% more PRs (10.1 PRs in Oct 2024 with no AI; 10.7 PRs per week in Oct 2026 with AI). An eye-catchingly small change!
  • The mean engineer shipped ~30% more PRs (11.1 PRs in Oct 2024 vs 14.8 PRs in Oct 2026)
  • Tenured engineers shipped ~70% more PRs (11.1 PRs in Oct 2024 vs 19 in Oct 2026)

New engineers are told to hold off on using AI for a month after they join. The AI SRE startup collected feedback from new engineers and found that new joiners using a lot of AI right after onboarding ended up performing worse in the medium/long term.

What incident.io found is that it’s worth ignoring expectations of shipping velocity during the first month. Instead, new devs learn how to navigate the codebase. This AI-abstinent approach skews the above numbers.

Harder to quantify: shipping faster & incidents

Compared to pre-AI, how important is it for PRs to be shipped faster to production? A benefit of AI agents and AI reviews is faster feedback than waiting on someone to review a PR. Here’s how quickly the median PR makes it to production at the reliability startup:

Let’s take an average day – a Tuesday last month – when 185 changes were shipped to production, 75 of which without human review:

There are fewer incidents per change, but more overall. It would be quite the omission to not bring up reliability when talking about a reliability startup! This is both good and bad news: there’s fewer incidents per PR, but more overall due to the existence of more PRs:

The good news is that the rate of incidents is lower than expected, given the PR volume:

The team looked into why incidents occurred, and found that most outages were because of incorrect code that could have been caught in review. The team took steps to address this:

  • Improved the codebase for AI use
  • Started leaning more on Cursor’s Bugbot, added stricter rules, and saw the tool start to give better feedback and catch more code-related bugs in review
  • Newer models produced better code.

Today, most incidents are no longer due to faulty code, but because there’s information absent about the production environment. The bad news is that if this continues and PR volume grows, then the number of incidents will also rise unless the team avoids outages related to production behavior. They are working on building feedback loops where agents can observe and learn from production.

I found these data points educational, especially looking at how the “cost per medium-sized PR” does (and probably should!) vary based on the complexity of work that goes into it. Thanks a lot to the incident.io team for sharing such detailed data!

Read the full issue of The Pulse from two weeks ago. The latest The Pulse covers:

  1. What can we learn from the Railway hack? Cloud platform Railway has published an extremely detailed postmortem about their recent hack in which the attacker likely used ‘abliterated’ AI models (those with no safeguards). Railway has hardened its systems as a result. Also, a competitor tried to benefit from the incident by getting Railway’s customers to migrate – but then got hacked itself in the exact same way.
  2. Native mobile and frontend jobs are disappearing. New data shows native mobile and frontend job listings are down by 50% at leading startups and Big Tech, while forward deployed engineer (FDE) listings have quadrupled in the same timeframe.
  3. How an extremely efficient engineering team works: Superlogical. Mitchell Hashimoto’s new startup is “AI-native” and cares deeply about craft and developer tools. They skip code reviews and commit to main thanks to deep trust between team members.
  4. Industry pulse. Jensen Huang no longer the CEO of NVIIDA, OpenAI buys Pierre Computer, Carta starts selling a coding harness, Meta buys and shuts down Conductor (a T3Code competitor), and Binance hacked with $6.3B stolen after devs were tricked into downloading packages and attending fake interviews.

item.title: The Pulse: Time to rethink software security because of AI?
item.description: A month’s worth of security breaches in a single day – will things get worse before they improve?
item.dc:creator: Ivan Klaric
item.content:encoded:
Hi, this is Gergely with a bonus, free issue of the Pragmatic Engineer Newsletter. In every issue, I cover Big Tech and startups through the lens of senior engineers and engineering leaders. Today, we cover one out of four topics from last week’s issue of The Pulse. Full subscribers received the article below eight days ago. If you’ve been forwarded this email, you can subscribe here.

It’s been an absolutely wild few days, with security breaches and major security vulnerabilities being exposed worldwide across tech. Many incidents took place on Tuesday and Wednesday of this week. We’ll start with a brief summary, then look closer at three of them:

  1. Intermediate CA certificate compromised: eight private 384-bit keys issued by eMudhra – which is an intermediate Certificate Authority (CAs) – leaked, meaning that servers in server-to-server communication can face man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks. Any internet communication not going through modern browsers (that already patched this) could be risky.
  2. PHP: Unpatched servers risk remote code execution (RCE) and opening up access for attackers. Around 70% of all websites run on PHP and unpatched systems are at risk. Two critical security patches have been released.
  3. Railway: customer secrets stored on the service were leaked and some have been decrypted. Secrets exposed can include access to production systems, enabling attackers to potentially access customer systems.
  4. GitLab: Unpatched GitLab servers are at risk of an attacker gaining full access. A critical security patch for RCE has been released.
  5. Node.js: Unpatched servers are vulnerable to remote execution attacks. A new release fixes 10 critical vulnerabilities (CVEs), including one that allows for RCE, and another fix revokes the compromised eMudhra intermediate certificate.
  6. Go: a new release is out, adding a mitigation for the compromised eMudhra intermediate certificate.
  7. TiDB: attackers gained near-total access to the complete control plane systems of the managed TiDB provider, PingCAP, for a whole month (!!). The attacker released 10TB of customer-sensitive data, including from Booking.com, Airbnb, Pinterest, Databricks, and more such as SQL queries that customers ran, billing, contacts, and source code for PingCAP’s systems The breach lasted from 9 Sept until 7 Oct, but was only disclosed this week. PingCAP claims no customer data stored inside TiDB was accessed, but I find it hard to see how the company will avoid losing security-conscious customers. This incident shows that the absence of adequate access monitoring and alerting can be an open invitation for attacks lasting weeks.

With that, let’s get into the first three incidents in the list.

eMudhra CA compromise

Certificate authorities (CAs) are organizations that vouch for identity on the internet. When a browser, phone, or server pings a site like chase.com or revolut.com, intermediate CAs and digital signatures verify that you really are talking with the bank’s server, and not a fake one set up by an attacker with the purpose of stealing users’ credentials. This is where the HTTPS protocol comes into play, with root CAs, intermediate CAs and the TLS handshake.

The whole system is built on a chain of trust and verification: we trust the root CAs and their certificates, and so we can trust the signatures of the intermediate CAs. The assumption is that both the root CA and intermediate CAs are trustworthy and verifiable.

But eMudhra broke this trust in the most blatant way: its private keys turned out to be single-digit numbers. A private key is a 384-bit key, which means that it would be a number between 0 and 2^384, (a number with 116 digits!)

Except, the key turned out to be the number “4.” Yes, that’s right: the number four. What on earth was eMudhra doing?! It’s as if they chose random numbers between 0 and 384, not 0 and 2^384! It is quite literally comical: in 2007, an XKCD comic described exactly this choice:

And the other keys were also not that much better: 56, 66, 115, 156, 230 and 237! It’s as if eMudhra generated an 8-bit private key, not a 384-bit one.

eMudhra explaining how these keys were generated (emphasis mine):

“We have done some preliminary assessment, there appears to be a flaw in the KGC [Key Generation Ceremony] script that was used on that specific day to create these ECC issuers. As for these ECC keys [elliptic-curve cryptography key pairs], our review of the KGC, assessment of the code and view of HSM [Hardware Security Module] keys so far indicate that a) a set of original ECC keys were created onboard as expected b) an approved deviation to our usual KGC to test a wrap/unwrap was introduced as these keys were meant for export for this instance c) a flaw in the code resulted in the second pair of keys being created onboard which were weaker d) these second pair of weaker keys were used by mistake to create the CSR [Certificate Signing Request] (because the key labels were similar) and signed by our root e) the CSR from these weaker keys were also sent over to Sectigo for cross signing (we verified the files sent over to Sectigo)

The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted.

Some additional context - these issuers were meant for export to our US and European data centers to solve data sovereignty issues for some of our customers (but never ended up operationally in production except for one).

We are still assessing the code to see steps where this process went wrong.”

I have so many questions:

  • How does eMudhra test generated keys? There seems to have been no automated testing of the key in place at all, in order to discover that these numbers were not “random” from a flaw in the key generation ceremony
  • How did eMudhra not notice this on day one, when the Key Generation Ceremony went wrong? If this was an automated process, the script would’ve changed from one day to the next, which would raise questions. If the process was fully manual, it explains how the mistake would be missed. And if it was manual, then why? Also, where are the detailed audits for such an important process?
  • The certificates with the easy-to-guess private keys were generated on 30 April 2025, so why did eMudhra not spot the mistake for 18 months?

Carelessness in the creation of intermediate certificates risks reputational damage to eMudhra’s business as a certificate authority. Google Chrome announced it is evaluating whether to continue with the company:

“Due to the seriousness of this incident, the Chrome Root Program is closely investigating the ongoing inclusion of eMudhra’s remaining CA certificates in the Chrome Root Store and will share further updates in public forums (e.g., the Common CA Database Public list) as our evaluation progresses.”

Given eMudhra’s sole business is in issuing digital certificates, being dropped by Chrome as a CA could be crippling. eMudhra is a publicly traded company on the Indian stock market, and two days before the breach was revealed its market cap was close to $500M. After details of its incompetence in creating certificates emerged, the company lost 40% of its value in two days.

PHP exploit: AI model beats attackers to finding critical vulnerability

The PHP situation is interesting because the “good guys” in this case (the security researchers) found a critical vulnerability in the framework before attackers did. From OpenAI:

“Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run websites and web applications. Calif [a respected security team] identified a critical flaw using GPT‑5.6 Sol as part of our Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window) initiative, with Wiz [a security company] also independently discovering and reporting both vulnerabilities. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with our teams and partners like Wiz, Cloudflare, and others contributing research, technical support, and coordination to prepare protections ahead of disclosure.”

On the surface, this is great news! Critical vulnerabilities were found and can now be patched, thereby closing the door before attackers can exploit them. Right..?

The problem of critical vulnerabilities for open source software is that systems which aren’t immediately patched can be exploited. When the PHP team released the fix for these two vulnerabilities, attackers got details about the vulnerabilities: the code itself shows where the attack can be inititiated! In the case of PHP, that means attackers can now easily execute remote code on any PHP server that is as yet unpatched.

Around 70% of all websites run PHP servers, which is a massive attack surface. We can be confident that many sites won’t update their PHP versions for days, weeks, months, or even years.

This particular vulnerability was so severe that before the security patch, the National Security Agency (NSA) in the US issued guidance urging websites to immediately patch upon release, or take applications fully offline until patched.

Exploits began hours before the fix was announced. It was known in advance that a major vulnerability fix was coming for PHP, and somehow, the vulnerability leaked from the group that disclosed and fixed it. Cloudflare was in the group that worked on this problem and created tooling to monitor and block exploit attempts. From Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince:

Amazon detected exploit attempts days before the fix. From AWS:

“Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.”

Attackers now have AI agents to automate and speed up attacks. Now that the vulnerability is known, attackers can simply spin up agents, instructing them to attempt to exploit servers that have not applied the patch. This probably explains why Cloudflare saw millions of exploit attempts just a few hours after the patch was released.

Railway’s customer secrets leak

Elsewhere on the same day, developer-first cloud provider Railway was hacked and the environment variables (secrets) of its customers were exposed. From the company:

“Our investigation to date indicates that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. Environment variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials.”

Immediately after detecting the breach, Railway took decisive action by notifying customers and the public, and pausing all deployments.

Pausing deployments created a huge headache for customers, who could not rotate their keys without crashing their systems running on Railway. Also from Railway:

“We strongly recommend that you immediately roll all environment variables, including any API keys, stored in Railway, as well as any private registry credentials, and review logs for those services for unusual activity.

All deployments are paused while we investigate. Until builds are restored, you will not be able to roll out new versions. We apologize for this inconvenience. Follow this incident to be notified when builds resume.”

This is contradictory: rotating environment variables – say, a database access token – means that the application using the old variable stops working until a redeploy. However, Railway has paused deploys! So, customers of Railway had two choices:

  • Rotate keys (the responsible step) and deliberately crash their application or take it offline (irresponsible)
  • Don’t rotate and hope their key was not leaked – (irresponsible) – and let their application continue to operate (responsible)

Of course, it’s clear why Railway is pausing deployments after the environment variables leaked, and the team must ensure that new variables added by customers do not leak.

In the end, it took Railway close to 20 hours to resolve the problem and allow deployments again. During that time, they unfortunately gave security-conscious customers an impossible choice of bricking their service while rotating keys, or ignoring security best practices to keep services running.

Can we expect future ‘deluges’ of security incidents?

AI labs did warn of a looming “security tsunami” fueled by the technology in May 2026, as per CNBC:

“Dario Amodei warned Tuesday [5 May 2026] that artificial intelligence has created a narrow window for the world’s tech firms, governments and banks to fix tens of thousands of software vulnerabilities found by his company’s latest model.

That AI model, Mythos, was previewed last month along with the disclosure that it had unearthed decades-old vulnerabilities in crucial software.

Since AI models from geopolitical adversary China are “maybe six to 12 months” behind the Anthropic product, there is “roughly that amount of time” to fix these issues, Amodei said.

“The danger is just some enormous increase in the amount of vulnerabilities, in the amount of breaches, in the financial damage that’s done from ransomware on schools, hospitals, not to mention banks,” Amodei said.

Anthropic has limited Mythos to a few partner companies because of concerns about what criminals or adversarial nations could do with it.”

Around that time, I talked with “AI-pilled” devs – some with access to the Mythos model – who told me the same: they expect the security landscape to become very bad in the coming months, with record numbers of systems being breached. One engineer said he’s moving many of his secrets like 2FA backup phrases off cloud storage services and onto paper because he expects cloud storage services to also be breached.

This week, it has seemed like the prediction in May has come to fruition, much of it done with AI’s help. A few days ago, on 17 October, OpenCode was breached and its customer secrets – AI API keys – stolen. Cofounder, Dax Raad, shared that the company has been under constant attack, in his reply to Railway:

Attacks much easier & defense much harder with AI

I sense the balance of power between the good and bad actors in this space is shifting because of AI. Let’s see what it took for an attacker to get access to a system before AI existed, via a critical vulnerability exposure (CVE) – disclosed or not:

With AI, finding critical vulnerabilities is easier for everybody, including bad actors who can automate attacks as well, and do so easily. The change:

It gets worse: before AI, it took quite some skill to be an effective attacker: you needed to be a good-enough coder, understand concepts like buffer overflows, and also learn techniques for executing remote code execution attacks. With AI, none of that applies. Venture capitalist, Deedy Das, described it as scary that nontechnical people now have the tools to easily exploit known CVEs like the PHP one:

So, let me update the diagram to account for the drastic lowering of the bar to becoming an effective attacker:

And we see all of this playing out in practice, starting with publicly disclosed CVEs skyrocketing:

We may need to urgently rethink software security for all systems:

  • Automated patching: manual monitoring for patches on a daily/weekly basis will become as irresponsible as applying patches months or years after release. Of course, automatic patching has its own risks, such as if a vendor providing a patch is breached, or a patch causes an outage, etc.
  • Expect attackers to use day-zero CVEs. Attackers will increasingly have access to undisclosed vulnerabilities and will access systems externally, or even execute code remotely.
  • Ongoing automated security monitoring to be non-negotiable. To detect security breaches, you need a decent level of automated logging and monitoring. This needs to be in place sooner rather than later. The TiDB incident this week shows what happens when a company allows an attacker to freely access their system for a month.
  • Defenders will have to use more AI. Attackers are gaining advantage by using AI agents, so defenders will have to do the same. There are no best practices in this field, but there are likely to be lessons in how companies like OpenCode, Railway, and PingCAP are responding – if they share their approaches.
  • Securing services and software will become more expensive. Continuously running AI agents to monitor for and mitigate breaches costs money, as do security engineers who are “AI-native.” This all increases the cost of security engineering. We previously covered security engineering basics and did a podcast on code security.

... and the security incidents continue

Since publishing the original article on 22 October, there have been more:

  • The Brotli remote execution CVE: Brotli is a compression library used at Node.js, Bun, Envoy, and others. The flaw allows an attacker to take over a service. Details
  • Another PHP remote code execution CVE. Just two days after the high-impact PHP2Shell patches, PHP warned of another important CVE, for which a fix is coming. PHP versions will need to be updated fast again.
  • Linux CVEs posted publicly. Several unpatched Linux kernel vulnerabilities were accidentally posted on the public kernel mailing list. Details.
  • Python Pillow CVE: a vulnerability inside the Python Pillow image library lets an attacker issue OS commands. Details
  • … and others I’ve doubtless missed.

At this rate, we might start getting “vulnerability fatigue” and become numb to critical security vulnerabilities unless they affect frameworks our applications use. To avoid that, it’ll be necessary for the industry to improve at coming up with and implementing security practices which work in a security environment where AI speeds up the discovery, publication, and exploitation of vulnerabilities.

Read the full issue of The Pulse this is from, or check out this week’s The Pulse. This week’s issue covers:

  1. Anthropic kills its coding interview. A team at the leading frontier AI company gets zero signal from DSA interviews and so has removed it from the engineering recruitment process. The rest of the company, and other AI-native startups, could follow.
  2. Details on incident.io’s AI spend and ROI. The resiliency startup has slashed the amount it spends on AI; down from $4,500 per dev, per month, in August, to $1,600 now.
  3. Amazon formally incorporates AI usage into SDE and SDM expectations. AI has been placed at the heart of software engineering after the company found a correlation between AI usage and productivity. Also, software development engineers (SDEs) and managers (SDMs) must be close to customers.
  4. Microsoft issues new exit offers to engineers. The tech giant has offered 60,000 employees the opportunity to quit by the end of the year. But the exit package is not particularly tempting, and so the number of people who take it will surely be in the thousands, not tens of thousands.

item.title: The Pulse: Anthropic builds its own source control system
item.description: Git had too many performance problems at 30,000 PRs per day, so Anthropic built its own. I talked with the team, including asking why they didn’t open source its new system, ‘Scion.’
item.dc:creator: Ivan Klaric
item.content:encoded:
Hi, this is Gergely with a bonus, free issue of the Pragmatic Engineer Newsletter. In every issue, I cover Big Tech and startups through the lens of senior engineers and engineering leaders. Today, we cover one out of four topics from last week’s issue of The Pulse. Full subscribers received the article below seven days ago. If you’ve been forwarded this email, you can subscribe here.

Interesting information from Anthropic about why the company moved off Git and built its own custom source control system. From their engineering blog (emphasis mine):

“At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.”

That’s a 12x increase in PRs in a four-month period! Interestingly, just a year ago, I shared how I had gathered Google was preparing for a similar tenfold increase across its broader infrastructure. From the deepdive published in July 2025:

“Google is preparing for 10x more code to be shipped. A former Google Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) told me: ‘What I’m hearing from SRE friends is that they are preparing for 10x the lines of code making their way into production.’

If any company has data on the likely impact of AI tools, it’s Google. 10x as much code generated will likely also mean 10x more code reviews, deployments, feature flags and source control footprint.”

Back to Anthropic, a few things about the company are different from many other tech businesses:

  • Use of a monorepo. Like most large tech companies, Anthropic has a massive monorepo, where the working copy itself is 25GB in size.
  • 25 million git checkouts per day, just for CI! All ~3,000 staff extensively use parallel Claude agents – typically 10-15 per engineer – so a lot of pull requests are created; somewhere in the region of 30,000 per day. All these PRs trigger a massive number of checkouts, mostly from the CI system.
  • Nearly all clients are always online. Git was built on the assumption that clients go offline at various times, and that when they come back up, they need to catch up with branches and merge their changes into the repo. However, when clients are always connected to the corporate internet – like at Anthropic – this assumption no longer holds. Design decisions to accommodate offline clients mean inefficient checkouts and more data transferred than necessary.
  • Hard to horizontally scale git. Scaling git is done by running git mirrors: replicating git repositories across several mirror nodes. A primary git server accepts the writes, pushes out to all mirrors, and clients fetch from various mirrors. Anthropic ran hundreds of git mirrors, but found that once their repo outgrew the mirrors’ disk capacity, they could no longer scale the repo.

So, Anthropic created a new source control system, which is called ‘Scion’ internally. It’s closed source, and Anthropic has shared the high-level design principles and data structures used, but no code details. The problem with having your own source control system (and moving off Git and GitHub) is that GitHub’s code review system is lost! So, Anthropic also had to build a new code review and code management system, which they call ‘Antique.’

I reached out to the team building Scion and Antique to learn more about how Scion works. Here’s what they told me:

Technical details

The design of Scion is pretty simple: stand up “server” nodes (that contain the whole repository), store changesets inside of Google Spanner (Google’s distributed, highly available database) and blobs (large files) in the highly durable Google Cloud Storage:

I asked Nick G – one of the authors of the original blog posts – about additional details and here’s what he told me:

  • Rust: the language that Scion’s server and client are written in.
  • Go + React: Antique, Anthropic’s new code review and code management platform has its backend in Go and frontend written in React. It works nicely with Scion.
  • More resilient replication strategy: by default, Google Spanner offers multi-zone replication with three replicas. Anthropic has increased the number of replicas (they didn’t tell me the exact number, but an educated guess could be five or more replicas), and switched to multi-region replication. All these changes make sense, given how critical code is and that it’s sensible to reduce the likelihood of losing any data – even at the cost of higher write latencies.
  • Backups: on top of replication, Anthropic keeps full backups of the database and soft deletes on the blob storage where file contents live. Spanner’s point-in-time recovery also lets Anthropic restore from a bad write. Smart!

Scaling is an interesting topic. I asked Nick if the system autoscales or scales manually. He told me:

“Every component can autoscale, but so far it hasn’t needed to, even as our merge volume grew more than 10x this year. The data is content-addressed and never changes once it’s stored, so the caching tiers do most of the work.”

A team of seven engineers builds and maintains all of this:

  • Four worked on the core Scion server and client
  • Three were split between building code search, merge queues, etc.

100% of Anthropic’s monorepo has moved off Git. This was no small feat to pull off! Nick gave me more details about the migration:

“The migration was not simple, but Claude was instrumental in getting it done. It’s also ‘self-healing’ in a way: if we get all the important use cases migrated and have something like 99% coverage, we can just force the cutover and Claude can help us fix anything that actually mattered.

100% of our monorepo is off of git. A few smaller repos that were never in the monorepo are migrating now, and they’re much simpler.

All of our community resources continue to live on GitHub: skills, plugins, Claude Code’s public repo, etc. And last week we launched OSS Scanner, which gives open-source projects free security audits using our strongest models (inspired by Google’s OSS-Fuzz).”

Big Tech moved off Git long ago

My take is that Anthropic has “Big Tech problems” much earlier than most of Big Tech had to tackle them. Anthropic employs around 3,500 staff, but their coding output – thanks to each person using around 10 agents all the time – is closer to that of a tech company with 35,000-70,000 staff! That’s a Meta or Google-sized company by the number of engineers.

Google and Meta have long since moved off Git because it did not scale for them.

Google built its own version control that took inspiration from Perforce. Git itself was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005, seven years after Google was founded. So git was not an option for Google to use in the early years: the company chose Perforce instead. It was around 2011-2012 that Google had ran into scaling issues with Perforce and built its own source control system called ‘Piper.’ It’s also a centralized version control model and still works well enough for the search giant. It’s no surprise to know that Piper was inspired by Perforce, and Google built Piper to be more performant for their use cases than Perforce was. We covered more on Google’s internal stack in the deepdive Inside Google’s Engineering Culture.

Meta found that git and other systems could not scale as needed, and so built ‘Sapling.’ Meta initially moved over to Mercurial, and then custom-built and open sourced Sapling for itself. As the company shared at the time:

“Sapling began 10 years ago [around 2012] as an effort to make Meta’s monorepo scale in the face of ever-increasing engineering growth. Publicly available source control systems were not, and still are not, capable of handling repositories of this size. Instead of moving away from the monorepo and sacrificing engineering velocity, we decided to build the source control system we needed.

Along the way we realized there were also large opportunities to increase developer velocity by improving the source control experience. By investing in new UX, we’ve made it possible for even new engineers to understand their repository and do things that were previously only possible for power users.”

Sapling itself is more of a client-server architecture. From the documentation:

“Sapling started from Mercurial as a distributed source control system, it then transitioned to a client-server architecture to solve the challenges. The server can utilize distributed storage and pre-build various kinds of indexes to provide more efficient operations.

While Sapling is less “distributed”, we tried to make the difference transparent to the user. For example, our lazy commit graph implementation does not require extra commands to “deepen” the graph. The user sees the full history.

That said, we do drop support of pulling from a lazy repo. Commit cloud covers these use-cases.”

Did Anthropic secretly rip off Sapling’s and Mononoke server

I asked Anthropic why it doesn’t open source Scion. Nick G’s reply:

“Mostly bandwidth! Even a no-support code drop takes a lot of work to do well. We have a small team building and running Scion. While the principles we used to build it are durable, the underlying code changes very frequently. For example, we’re still removing git-compatibility layers we only needed for the migration. We’d rather put that time into sharing what we learned, and as the post says, into working with GitHub, GitLab and the OSS community on scaling git.

To emphasize that point: most teams don’t need to leave git! But we think there are things git could benefit from, mainly change sets, derived data, and the checkout protocol. Our goal was to inspire conversation and collaboration around those ideas.”

The explanation, on one end, makes sense. On the other, Meta themselves also emphasized how most teams don’t need to leave git, and still open sourced Sapling for anyone to use, or take inspiration from.

One key component of Sapling is Monoke: the also open source server meant to scale up accepting thousands of commits every hour, across millions of files, written in Rust.

Could have Anthropic avoided open sourcing Scion, because it might have shown how much they copied from existing open source projects? The creator of Monoke wrote a post accusing of the Anthropic team of ripping off Monoke — and the Bonsai data model — writing:

“This [Scion] was a ripoff. My post yesterday was trying to be as charitable as possible given what I knew, and in particular that the similarity to Mononoke was mostly unintentional and the lack of credit was the result of not doing due diligence. However, after publishing the post I privately received confirmation that Scion intentionally and blatantly ripped off Mononoke, and in particular that there was overlap in personnel. There is no chance that this was an unintentional homage. This is something I had a hunch about but was not comfortable saying yesterday, given what I knew back then.

The resemblance is much deeper than just the notion of derived data. Some people pointed out that derived data is just an index, which is a well-known concept. I want to clarify that derived data was merely the most striking resemblance. It goes much deeper than that, and extends to the entire data model, as well as a number of the structures built around it.”

Anthropic did not give credit to Monoke in their original post, and only added a small attribution after the complaint.

To be clear, the point of open source is that you can do what you want with the software without much limitations (save for what the license contains): but it’s poor form that it took a public complaint for Anthropic to admit that the clever data structure they presented in their blog post heavily derived for an existing and open source data strucutre.

Will central VCs stay a niche, or expland beyond Big Tech?

Big Tech has preferred centralized version control systems (VCS), and I wonder how niche of a trend central VCSs will remain. As we’ve seen since well before AI, some of the largest tech companies dropped git because they did not like the performance degradation from offline support they no longer need.

My question is that even with agents, how many companies will see git “break” similarly to how it has at Anthropic? When this happens, how many will find git’s mirroring functionality inadequate for their own needs?

There’s a new batch of vendors positioning themselves as git-compatible version control solutions built for AI scale: Entire, founded by GitHub’s last CEO, Thomas Dohmke (a current podcast season sponsor), Cursor Origin by SpaceX, and Code Storage by The Pierre Company. At the same time, GitHub itself seems to be investing a lot more in making its platform more reliable and scalable.

My hunch is that very few companies will go through the trouble of building yet another source control system. In this way, Anthropic reminds me a bit of Google, which has been known to build custom internal systems which are not publicly available, to address the company’s internal needs. This can be disorienting for Google engineers after they leave the company and find they’ve become out of touch with industry-standard tools.
